frictionVectors.title: European energy leverage
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over oil and gas assets, but European demand and infrastructure links create leverage over export policy and pricing.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara and Morocco rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Regional tensions constrain transport, trade, and energy integration across the Maghreb, limiting Algeria's broader strategic options.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Angola is strengthening state oversight and seeking investment beyond oil, but foreign operators and declining mature fields still shape revenue and production decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure has expanded connectivity while creating long-term repayment and strategic-dependence concerns around major projects.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity near the Burkina Faso and Niger borders threatens transport corridors, agricultural production, and state access to frontier resources.

frictionVectors.title: Regional trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: Benin's port economy remains exposed to relations with Nigeria and neighboring Sahel states, giving larger regional powers influence over customs and transit flows.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers partnership tensions
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has improved its share of diamond value and marketing influence, but negotiations with De Beers remain central to national revenue and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: New interest in copper, nickel, and other minerals could diversify the economy, while also increasing pressure from foreign investors for favorable concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Mining renegotiation under insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking greater state participation and local processing in gold, but insurgent violence and informal mining limit effective control over production zones.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The shift away from French security ties toward Russian support increases room for sovereign maneuver but creates new dependence on an external security provider.

highlights: Gold and 3TG exports remain weakly governed

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL SMUGGLING
frictionVectors.details: Gold and tin, tantalum and tungsten supply chains remain vulnerable to informal extraction, cross-border smuggling and opaque intermediaries. Limited state capacity reduces Burundi's ability to capture full value from its mineral base.

frictionVectors.title: REGIONAL ACCESS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Burundi relies heavily on transport corridors through Tanzania and neighboring states for external trade. Regional tensions involving Rwanda and eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo increase exposure to border disruption and security pressure.

highlights: Tourism and foreign finance shape autonomy

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND MARITIME COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's ports, airspace and maritime position attract competing external investment and security partnerships. The government must balance economic benefits against strategic dependence on foreign operators and donors.

frictionVectors.title: TOURISM CONCENTRATION
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on tourism, remittances and imported energy leaves the economy exposed to external shocks. This constrains policy autonomy even as institutions retain comparatively strong control over national assets.

highlights: Oil, gas and timber remain externally contested

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE CONCESSION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and state-linked investors remain central to oil, gas, mining, timber and major infrastructure projects. Contract opacity and limited domestic processing weaken Cameroon's ability to convert resources into broad sovereign gains.

frictionVectors.title: ANGLOPHONE INFRASTRUCTURE RISK
frictionVectors.details: Separatist violence continues to threaten roads, plantations, energy assets and commercial logistics in the Northwest and Southwest. Persistent insecurity increases the leverage of external security and infrastructure partners.

highlights: Russian security ties anchor external influence

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY-RESOURCE NEXUS
frictionVectors.details: Russian security personnel and aligned commercial networks remain influential around regime protection and extractive activity. This can expand government control in some areas while reducing transparency and bargaining power over mineral concessions.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CORRIDOR FRAGMENTATION
frictionVectors.details: Gold and diamond production is dispersed across insecure zones and informal routes toward neighboring markets. Weak transport infrastructure and armed-group taxation prevent the state from exercising consistent control over extraction and trade.

highlights: Oil revenues underpin a centralized state
Sudan war strains borders and corridors

frictionVectors.title: OIL AND PIPELINE LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal and political system remains heavily dependent on oil production and export infrastructure operated with foreign technical and financial involvement. Revenue volatility and contract dependence limit long-term sovereign resource planning.

frictionVectors.title: SUDAN BORDER SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: The war in Sudan has intensified refugee flows, arms risks and cross-border insecurity in eastern Chad. External actors and armed networks can exploit the pressure on humanitarian, military and transport infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: FRANCE–MAYOTTE DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: France’s control of Mayotte remains a central sovereignty grievance and limits Comoros’ ability to shape maritime and migration policy around the archipelago.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Port, energy, and transport development depends heavily on external partners, leaving the government with limited leverage over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTRACT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and state-backed investors retain major influence over copper and cobalt value chains, while weak refining capacity limits domestic capture of strategic-resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: EASTERN SECURITY CORRIDOR
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and regional actors continues to threaten mining zones, transport routes, and Kinshasa’s control over eastern territory and resources.

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON CONCENTRATION
frictionVectors.details: Public finances remain highly exposed to oil production and external operators, constraining diversification and increasing vulnerability to price and contract pressures.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND DEBT LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure and Pointe-Noire’s strategic role strengthen connectivity but can narrow fiscal and policy autonomy when debt service and project terms become binding.

frictionVectors.title: COCOA PROCESSING CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan is expanding local processing and farmer protections, but multinational buyers and volatile global pricing still limit national control over the cocoa value chain.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE ENERGY PARTNERSHIPS
frictionVectors.details: New oil and gas development improves energy security and fiscal prospects while increasing reliance on foreign capital, technology, and long-term production agreements.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN BASE COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The concentration of foreign military facilities provides revenue and security guarantees but subjects Djibouti to competing external agendas and regional escalation risks.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND DEBT EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti’s ports and logistics corridors are central to its economic model, yet foreign ownership, financing, and debt obligations constrain autonomous control of strategic infrastructure.

highlights: Nile security remains the strategic priority

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile Water Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose unilateral Ethiopian management of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and seeks binding rules for drought years. The dispute remains a major sovereignty and regional-security concern.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF support and Gulf investment stabilize Egypt’s finances but increase outside leverage over asset sales, infrastructure priorities, and economic policy.

highlights: Diversification is constrained by declining output

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Equatorial Guinea retains formal control over hydrocarbons but relies heavily on foreign operators, technology, and markets. Falling production heightens pressure to attract new external capital.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Large state-led construction projects have strengthened regime control but remain vulnerable to contractor dependence, debt exposure, and limited public oversight.

highlights: State control over strategic assets remains strong
Mining provides leverage but narrows autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Mining Partnership Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc projects provide revenue and foreign exchange, yet require external operators, financing, and technical capacity. Commodity concentration limits the practical depth of sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Militarization
frictionVectors.details: Tensions involving Ethiopia, Sudan, and Red Sea security keep Eritrea’s strategic environment volatile. External military competition and sanctions risk constrain its room for maneuver.

highlights: Economic sovereignty remains tied to South Africa
Sugar and manufacturing anchor limited diversification

frictionVectors.title: South African Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini depends heavily on South Africa for trade, transport corridors, customs revenue, energy links, and investment. This creates substantial external leverage over domestic economic resilience.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and Agribusiness Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Sugar exports and related infrastructure remain important sources of foreign exchange but are exposed to international pricing, market-access rules, and foreign-owned supply chains.

highlights: Debt and conflict constrain economic sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Nile and GERD Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: The dam expands Ethiopia’s control over electricity generation and regional power exports while sustaining acute tensions with Egypt and Sudan. Financing, transmission, and export markets still require external partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on Chinese, Gulf, Turkish, and multilateral financing limit Addis Ababa’s policy autonomy. Conflict-related damage and fiscal pressure also threaten control over critical transport and energy assets.

highlights: Manganese and oil remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater domestic participation and value addition in manganese, iron ore, and oil. This may generate friction with established French, Chinese, and other foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors and logistics remain concentrated around foreign-backed infrastructure and operators, limiting Gabon's leverage over resource flows despite stronger political control.

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegalese territory, transport links, and regional security cooperation. Border and transit disruptions can quickly affect food supplies, commerce, and fuel access.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-owned tourism exposure
frictionVectors.details: Hotels, aviation, and tourism demand are strongly controlled or influenced by external investors and European markets. Economic sovereignty remains constrained by seasonal capital and visitor flows.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and critical-minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: Ghana retains substantial gold capacity but continues to confront illicit mining, environmental damage, and foreign-linked smuggling networks. Emerging lithium development could reproduce a pattern of exporting raw materials without sufficient domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: IMF-linked fiscal constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF conditions are narrowing fiscal room for infrastructure and industrial policy. External creditors and investors retain significant influence over the pace and design of economic reforms.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mining corridors
frictionVectors.details: Large Chinese, Western, and multinational consortia dominate capital-intensive bauxite and iron-ore projects. Rail, port, and power infrastructure tied to these projects may increase exports without proportionate domestic industrial gains.

frictionVectors.title: Junta uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: The military government uses resource nationalism to build legitimacy while delaying a clear political transition. Contract reviews and opaque decision-making raise risks for investors, communities, and neighboring states.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy depends heavily on raw cashew exports, leaving farmers and state revenue exposed to foreign buyers, price swings, and limited domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Narco-trafficking and security penetration
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and political fragmentation leave the country vulnerable to transnational cocaine networks and external security influence. This undermines control of ports, airstrips, and maritime territory.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Strategic Assets
frictionVectors.details: Kenya's financing relationships with China, Gulf investors, and multilateral lenders constrain fiscal autonomy. Concerns persist over the long-term control and revenue allocation of transport and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Port Competition and Regional Trade
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa faces competition from Tanzania's ports as regional states seek alternatives and external partners pursue logistics influence. This rivalry affects Kenya's leverage over landlocked neighbors and corridor revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Water Export Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water infrastructure and export revenues remain deeply tied to South Africa, limiting its bargaining autonomy. Proposed transfers and dam projects generate recurring concerns over compensation, displacement, and national control.

frictionVectors.title: Industrial and Fiscal Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The textile sector and customs revenues are vulnerable to external trade preferences and South African economic conditions. Foreign-owned production provides employment but leaves limited domestic control over value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Mining Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Liberia depends heavily on foreign mining firms for investment, exports, and infrastructure, while the state captures only a portion of the resource value. Contract renegotiation, local employment, and environmental oversight remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia and mining-linked rail corridors attract competing external commercial interests. Weak state capacity makes infrastructure concessions vulnerable to opaque terms and limited domestic downstream benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Divided Control of Oil Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to use oil fields, export terminals, and budget access as instruments of bargaining. International oil companies and foreign governments retain influence through production, contracting, and mediation channels.

frictionVectors.title: Competing External Military Influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked forces, and other regional actors sustain competing security relationships around Libya's bases, coast, and energy infrastructure. This limits national control over strategic territory and complicates reunification of state institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Large nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mining projects are dominated by foreign capital and exposed to volatile global prices. Madagascar faces persistent challenges in securing local processing, fiscal returns, and credible environmental enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Commodity Chain Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The vanilla economy and emerging critical-mineral exports leave rural incomes and foreign exchange vulnerable to external buyers and logistics disruptions. Weak transport infrastructure increases the bargaining power of foreign traders and concession operators.

highlights: Uranium and Agriculture Seek New Capital

frictionVectors.title: IMF-Linked Austerity
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-backed reforms are narrowing fiscal autonomy while fuel, fertilizer, and foreign-exchange shortages expose Malawi to external financing conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Mineral Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The restart and expansion of uranium and other mining projects depend heavily on foreign operators, capital, and offtake agreements, limiting domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-Sector Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is pressing foreign mining companies for larger state returns and tighter control, but legal uncertainty and insecurity threaten production and investment.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security forces and commercial networks is reducing Western influence while creating opaque channels around mining access, logistics, and state sovereignty.

highlights: Iron Ore Still Anchors the State

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers major export revenue but leaves Mauritania dependent on foreign operators, maritime infrastructure, and cross-border coordination with Senegal.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Resource Logistics
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, ports, and prospective green-hydrogen projects rely on external capital and export corridors, raising concerns over local processing and long-term value retention.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Settlement Implementation
frictionVectors.details: The sovereignty transition over the Chagos Archipelago remains strategically sensitive, particularly around the Diego Garcia military facility and future security arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Import and Connectivity Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius retains strong state capacity but remains vulnerable to external fuel, food, shipping, and tourism shocks, alongside competition among Indian, Chinese, Gulf, and Western partners.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries, ports, and renewable projects in Western Sahara remain central to Morocco's sovereignty strategy and a continuing source of friction with Algeria and Polisario supporters.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Security
frictionVectors.details: Drought and water stress are increasing dependence on desalination, imported energy, and large foreign-backed infrastructure projects even as Morocco expands renewables and domestic industrial capacity.

highlights: Mining corridors attract competing external capital

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado security and LNG access
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to threaten northern communities and delay the full development of offshore gas projects. Foreign security assistance and energy investment remain central to Mozambique's ability to convert resources into sovereign revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-mineral project dependency
frictionVectors.details: Coal, graphite and other mining operations rely heavily on foreign firms, logistics networks and export corridors. Weak domestic processing limits local value capture and increases exposure to external commercial pressure.

highlights: Oil discoveries reshape national bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: Offshore oil discoveries have increased Namibia's leverage but also created competition among international energy companies for exploration and development rights. Fiscal terms and local-content rules will determine whether the discoveries strengthen domestic sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic minerals and power infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Uranium, lithium and rare-earth projects are drawing external investors while Namibia remains dependent on regional electricity links and imported equipment. Limited domestic refining and grid capacity could reduce the country's bargaining power.

highlights: Export routes and sanctions remain vulnerable

frictionVectors.title: Oil pipeline sovereignty dispute
frictionVectors.details: Niger's access to crude-export infrastructure through neighboring states remains exposed to diplomatic conflict, sanctions and commercial disputes. The government seeks greater control over petroleum revenues, but landlocked logistics constrain its options.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and external security competition
frictionVectors.details: The authorities are renegotiating long-standing relationships in the uranium sector while seeking alternative political and security partners. Reduced Western assistance and expanding Russian influence create uncertainty over investment, security guarantees and operational capacity.

highlights: Grid and pipeline insecurity erode resource gains

frictionVectors.title: Oil theft and pipeline sabotage
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, vandalism and insecurity continue to reduce production and public revenue despite efforts to improve regulation and monitoring. Foreign operators retain major technical and financial roles, limiting Abuja's control over the full value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-mineral investment imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed projects are expanding in lithium and other minerals, but weak processing capacity and regulatory enforcement risk repeating the country's raw-export model. Power shortages and transport bottlenecks further constrain domestic value addition.

highlights: Regional security ties trigger external pressure

frictionVectors.title: Conflict minerals and eastern Congo exposure
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's mineral-trading position and alleged links to armed actors in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo remain major sources of diplomatic and commercial pressure. Sanctions scrutiny and regional tensions could affect access to markets and investment.

frictionVectors.title: Aid, finance and strategic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Kigali retains strong administrative control over domestic development priorities but remains reliant on external aid, concessional finance and foreign investment. Western criticism over regional security policies could narrow that financial space.

frictionVectors.title: Deepwater licensing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Exploration in the jointly managed Nigeria–São Tomé and Príncipe Zone remains commercially uncertain, creating pressure to attract foreign operators without weakening revenue safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Limited naval capacity leaves the archipelago dependent on external partners and regional mechanisms to protect fisheries, offshore prospects, and shipping routes.

frictionVectors.title: Contract and revenue renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking stronger domestic control and transparency in hydrocarbons and mining, increasing tension with international operators and lenders over existing agreements.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-financed infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Major transport and energy projects depend on external finance, leaving Dakar exposed to creditor conditions while it tries to preserve policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing access
frictionVectors.details: Licensing arrangements with distant-water fleets generate revenue but continue to raise concerns over stock depletion, monitoring capacity, and the distribution of maritime benefits.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, energy, and connectivity projects rely on foreign capital and partnerships, requiring careful balancing among India, China, Gulf actors, and Western donors.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mining dependency
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led iron ore operations remain central to export earnings, leaving the state vulnerable to commodity cycles, contract disputes, and limited domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese-backed infrastructure footprint
frictionVectors.details: External financing and construction partnerships expand roads, energy, and port capacity but raise concerns over debt exposure, procurement transparency, and strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime access competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign security and infrastructure partnerships around ports and maritime zones are expanding, while disputes over federal authority and regional agreements complicate sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Resource insecurity and illicit extraction
frictionVectors.details: Weak enforcement enables illegal fishing, charcoal trafficking, and unregulated resource activity, while international security assistance remains essential to protect trade and offshore prospects.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and port constraints
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and congestion at Durban and other freight corridors continue to weaken South Africa's ability to process and export resources on sovereign terms.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for battery and platinum-group mineral access, creating leverage but also pressure over investment conditions and beneficiation.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-route dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on Sudanese export infrastructure, leaving production and public finances exposed to conflict, pipeline disruption, and bargaining by external operators.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security influence
frictionVectors.details: Internal factional tensions and the involvement of neighboring states constrain sovereign control over territory, transport corridors, and natural-resource revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Externalized civil war
frictionVectors.details: Competing foreign patrons and regional networks are sustaining rival armed coalitions, reducing state control over gold, agricultural zones, and key transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Port and gold competition
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan and informal gold flows is central to wartime financing, while outside powers seek influence over Red Sea access and mineral supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor bargaining
frictionVectors.details: The expansion of Dar es Salaam and Central Corridor infrastructure is attracting Gulf, Chinese, and Western interest, increasing Tanzania's leverage while raising concerns about long-term concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and mining terms
frictionVectors.details: Negotiations over offshore gas and large-scale mining continue to balance foreign capital needs against local-content, revenue-sharing, and environmental demands.

frictionVectors.title: Port concession exposure
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's role as a transshipment and Sahel supply hub brings revenue and strategic relevance, but also dependence on foreign shipping, logistics, and terminal operators.

frictionVectors.title: Northern corridor insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist spillover from the Sahel threatens roads and border communities, complicating state control over northern trade routes and resource access.

frictionVectors.title: Migration-Finance Bargain
frictionVectors.details: European funding and market access remain closely tied to migration control, giving external partners substantial leverage over Tunisian policy. Fiscal pressure limits Tunis's room to negotiate from strength.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and Phosphate Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported energy and underperforming phosphate production. Foreign-backed renewable and infrastructure projects could improve resilience but may deepen dependence without stronger domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Sovereignty Clash
frictionVectors.details: The Tilenga-EACOP oil system is advancing with major foreign corporate and state financing, while environmental, land, and human-rights disputes remain acute. Uganda gains export infrastructure but retains limited control over technology, finance, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Funded Connectivity
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, energy, and industrial projects strengthen connectivity but increase exposure to external creditors and contractors. Local-content gains remain uneven.

frictionVectors.title: Copper Ownership Tension
frictionVectors.details: New investment is expanding copper production and restoring strategic assets, but foreign operators still dominate capital, technology, and export channels. Zambia is seeking more processing and fiscal value without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Power-System Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages constrain mining and industrial sovereignty, while drought and dependence on regional power imports increase vulnerability. Grid rehabilitation and renewable projects remain reliant on external finance.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Bargain
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is restricting raw lithium exports to encourage domestic processing, but Chinese-linked capital and technology retain a strong position across the battery-minerals chain. Limited financing and weak industrial capacity constrain effective sovereign value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Parallel Gold Economy
frictionVectors.details: Gold and diamond sectors remain vulnerable to smuggling, opaque intermediaries, and politically connected networks. Sanctions, currency instability, and external trading channels reduce the state's ability to secure transparent revenue.
